hints: Focus on who can give electrons and who can take them, think about which of these pollutants is a good reducing agent and which is a good oxidising agent.
Notice that in $\text{SO}_2$ sulfur is in oxidation state +4 and can still be oxidised up to +6, while in $\text{NO}_2$ nitrogen is in +4 and can easily be reduced to +2 in $\text{NO}$.
Check which pairing lets one pollutant be oxidised while the other is reduced, and remember that $\text{CO}_2$ with carbon already at +4 cannot act as an oxidant.
walkthrough:
**Sort out oxidising and reducing power**

Think like a teacher with your redox hats on. A reducing agent gets oxidised itself, and an oxidising agent gets reduced itself.

Oxidation number check:
$$\text{S in SO}_2 = +4 \to \text{S in SO}_3 = +6$$
$$\text{N in NO}_2 = +4 \to \text{N in NO} = +2$$

**Test the possible partnerships**

$\text{SO}_2$ is a well known reducing agent in the atmosphere because S(+4) wants to go to S(+6). $\text{NO}_2$ is a well known oxidising agent because N(+4) can drop to N(+2).

Put them together:
$$\text{SO}_2 + \text{NO}_2 \to \text{SO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

**Rule out the impossible partners**

$\text{CO}$ is not spontaneously oxidised by oxygen in clean air, it needs hydroxyl radicals or a catalyst. $\text{CO}_2$ cannot oxidise $\text{SO}_2$ because carbon is already at its maximum +4, so it has no oxidising power left.

So the only feasible atmospheric redox is $\text{SO}_2$ reducing $\text{NO}_2$.

options.A: CO to $\text{CO}_2$ is oxidation, but it is not spontaneous in the atmosphere. It is slow and requires hydroxyl radicals or catalysts, so this is a common overgeneralisation trap.
options.B: This is correct. $\text{SO}_2$ acts as the reducing agent (oxidised to $\text{SO}_3$) and $\text{NO}_2$ acts as the oxidising agent (reduced to NO). This is an important atmospheric reaction leading toward acid rain formation.
options.C: Although CO is a reducing agent and $\text{NO}_2$ is an oxidising agent on paper, this specific reduction of $\text{NO}_2$ to NO by CO does not occur significantly in the atmosphere. Students often pick this by redox logic alone without recalling the observed atmospheric chemistry.
options.D: $\text{SO}_2$ to $\text{SO}_3$ is oxidation, but $\text{CO}_2$ cannot be the oxidant. Carbon in $\text{CO}_2$ is already +4, its highest oxidation state, so it cannot be reduced further to oxidise something else.
